claims.claim: Vocabulary knowledge is key to reading comprehension: readers cannot understand what they are reading without knowing what most of the words mean.
Most vocabulary is learned indirectly through everyday encounters with spoken and written language, while some words must be taught directly.
Prefixes attach to the beginning of a base word and change its meaning; common English prefixes include un- (not or reverse), re- (again), dis- (reverse or remove), and inter- (between).
Suffixes attach to the end of a base word and usually change its meaning or part of speech; suffixes such as -tion often form nouns from verbs and -ful often forms adjectives.
Morphology is the study of how words are built from roots, prefixes, and suffixes and of how words relate to one another; understanding word parts reduces reliance on rote memorization.
Word families group words built from the same base with different affixes; word webs with the base at the centre and related forms in spokes make those connections visible.
A collocation is a combination of words that are often used together in a way that sounds natural; collocations range from fixed, with little choice of partner word, to freer, with more options.
Collocations often have to be memorised, and recording them in a notebook when they are met helps learners keep them.
There are four main kinds of word formation in English: prefixes, suffixes, conversion, and compounds.

Vocabulary is often described in layers: the everyday high-frequency core, academic words (the Academic Word List contains 570 word families outside the most frequent 2,000 words of English, selected for learners preparing for tertiary study), and field-specific technical words served by purpose-built lists such as those used in English for specific purposes.

A practical framework for deliberate vocabulary growth is the four-step cycle of encounter, understand, use, and review; each step maps to sourced practice (meeting words in reading and listening, checking meaning and word parts, producing the word in speaking or writing, and recording and revisiting it).

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much vocabulary growth comes from indirect exposure versus direct instruction.
positions: Research on vocabulary instruction shows most vocabulary is learned indirectly, through everyday experiences with oral and written language.
Some vocabulary must be taught directly, especially words representing complex concepts that learners rarely meet on their own.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the two as complementary: wide reading and listening supply most encounters, while deliberate attention — word parts, chunks, journals, and review — targets the words exposure alone will not secure.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether vocabulary is 'the single biggest predictor' of reading comprehension.
positions: Popular reading-science summaries describe vocabulary as the single best predictor of comprehension.

The verified source used here (Reading Rockets) states that vocabulary is key to reading comprehension and that readers cannot understand a text without knowing what most of its words mean, without ranking it against other factors.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the verified wording — vocabulary is key to reading comprehension — and does not assert an unverified ranking.

unsupportedExistingClaims: 'Vocabulary Building is a foundational concept in Languages & Esl' — generic machine-generated boilerplate with no source support.

sourceRecords.title: Vocabulary/Morphology – Prefixes — Language Foundations Handbook
sourceRecords.provider: eCampusOntario Open Library (Ruth McQuirter and Carolyn Venema)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per the subject source map (eCampusOntario Language Foundations). Read live on 2026-08-21 via curl (HTTP 200). Supports: prefixes as morphemes that precede a base to form a different word; negative prefixes (un-, non-, dis-, in-, im-, ir-), number prefixes (uni-, bi-, tri-, quad-, penta-, semi-), and direction prefixes (trans-, sub-, inter-); free bases (eat, date, week) versus bound bases (-ject in inject/project); the act base family (acted, action, activity, activate, react); morphological knowledge as impacting reading, writing, and vocabulary and reducing reliance on memorization. Reference only; all lesson examples are original.

sourceRecords.title: Vocabulary/Morphology – Suffixes — Language Foundations Handbook
sourceRecords.provider: eCampusOntario Open Library (Ruth McQuirter and Carolyn Venema)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per the subject source map. Read live on 2026-08-21 via curl (HTTP 200). Supports: suffixes as morphemes added to the end of a base to create a different (derived) word; suffixes usually changing the meaning and/or part of speech of the base; morphology as the study of word structures and patterns (prefixes, roots, suffixes) and of how words relate to one another; word webs with the base at the centre and related forms in spokes; spelling changes when suffixes are added (excite/excitement, happy/happiness). Reference only; no source wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Prefixes — Cambridge Dictionary Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (Cambridge Dictionary named in the subject source map). Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: prefixes attaching to the beginning of a base word and changing its meaning; prefixes making a word negative or expressing relations of time, place, or manner; the common-prefix table including un- (not/reverse), re- (again), dis- (reverse/remove), inter- (between), sub- (under/below), pre- (before). Reference only; lesson examples (unkind, unlock, rebuild, retell, disconnect, intercity) are original.

sourceRecords.title: Suffixes — Cambridge Dictionary Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: a suffix as a letter or group of letters added at the end of a word to make a new word, most often of a different word class; -ful changing verbs to adjectives (forgetful, useful); -ion/-tion changing verbs to nouns (complication, creation); spelling changes when suffixes are added; a good learner's dictionary as the check for suffix spelling. Reference only; lesson examples (celebration, information, careful, colourful) are original.

sourceRecords.title: Word formation — Cambridge Dictionary Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports the four main kinds of word formation: prefixes, suffixes, conversion (email, microwave as verbs from nouns), and compounds. Used for the word-formation framing only; reference only, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Collocation — Cambridge Dictionary (English definition)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports the definition of collocation as the combination of words formed when two or more words are often used together in a way that sounds natural ('a hard frost'), and the grammar note that collocation refers to how words go together or form fixed relationships. Reference only; lesson examples (make a decision, heavy traffic, catch a cold) are original.

sourceRecords.title: Collocation — TeachingEnglish (British Council)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (British Council TeachingEnglish named in the subject source map). The live site resets or times out automated connections, so the page was read via an Internet Archive capture of 2015-06-28 (web.archive.org/web/20150628035944/http://www.teachingenglish.org.uk/article/collocation); the canonical live URL is registered. Supports: collocation as words that are found together in language; fixed collocations (little choice of partner word) versus freer collocations (more choice); collocations often having to be memorised; teachers helping learners record collocations in notebooks. Reference only; all lesson examples are original.

sourceRecords.title: What do ESP teachers need to know about word lists for language learning and teaching? — TeachingEnglish (British Council)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. The live site resets automated connections; read via an Internet Archive capture of 2016-04-07 (web.archive.org/web/20160407083208/http://www.teachingenglish.org.uk/article/what-do-esp-teachers-need-know-about-word-lists-language-learning-teaching); the canonical live URL is registered. Supports the modest claim that word lists are built for specific purposes — the IATEFL ESP SIG and British Council joint event page centres on using and evaluating word lists in English for specific purposes, with Averil Coxhead's Academic Word List (2000) as the springboard. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Basics: Vocabulary — Reading Rockets (Reading 101)
sourceRecords.notes: Reputable secondary source (Tier D); WETA is a public broadcaster and the site is a widely used reading-research reference. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: vocabulary as key to reading comprehension ('readers cannot understand what they are reading without knowing what most of the words mean'); the scientific finding that most vocabulary is learned indirectly through everyday oral and written language with some words needing direct instruction; listening, speaking, reading, and writing vocabulary types; analyzing word parts (e.g., root words) as a direct word-learning strategy. Reference only; prose fully synthesized.
